title: XIL: Cross-Expanding Incremental Learning
claim: Prior incremental learning keeps one domain per task and evaluates narrowly; ours spans domains and expands class-domain associations in both directions.
layout: 2×2 grid: CIL left, XIL right; training top, inference bottom; dashed divider
description: The figure compares conventional class-incremental learning (CIL, left) with the proposed cross-expanding incremental learning (XIL, right). A dashed vertical line separates the two. The top row shows training and the bottom row shows inference. Each panel is a grid of class columns (C1, C2, ..., Ct) and domain rows (D1, D2, ..., Dt). The images show the same classes (airplane, alarm clock, axe, basketball, bicycle, bird) drawn in different styles: clipart, infographic, sketch. In CIL training, black boxes cover only the D1 row, and orange arrows move across classes. In XIL training, black boxes step diagonally through the domains, with arrows between them. Unselected cells are faded. In inference, a red box covers a single row for CIL. For XIL it covers the whole class-by-domain grid. Legend in the middle explains the black and red boxes.
caption: Comparison of training and inference phases between conventional class-incremental learning (CIL) and our proposed cross-expanding incremental learning (XIL). While CIL assumes a shared domain across all incremental tasks, XIL considers distinct domains and requires bidirectional semantic expansion, extending new classes to past domains and past classes to new ones.
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) traditionally assumes that all tasks share a similar domain distribution, limiting its applicability in real-world scenarios where data arrive from evolving environments. We introduce a new problem setting, Cross-Expanding Incremental Learning (XIL), which extends CIL by requiring models to handle class-incremental data across distinct domains and to expand class-domain associations bidirectionally. In this setting, new classes should be integrated into previously seen domains, while earlier classes are extended to newly encountered ones, a capability we refer to as bidirectional domain transferability (BiDoT). To address XIL, we present a new framework, Semantic Expansion through Evolving Domains (XEED), which leverages domain-specialized prompts, residual-guided representation modulation, and evolving prototype embeddings to expand class semantics across previously encountered domains. We further introduce the BiDoT Score, a novel metric for quantifying the degree of BiDoT. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets with significant domain shifts demonstrate that XEED outperforms existing CIL baselines by a large margin in both standard accuracy and BiDoT scores, establishing a strong foundation for realistic continual learning under domain-evolving conditions.
